blocks.text: Every sort so far compares two values at a time, and comparison sorts can't beat O(n log n). **Counting sort** and **radix sort** never compare values at all — they use each value (or each digit) as an **index**. When values are small integers, or have a fixed number of digits, that makes sorting linear.

blocks.alt: Counting sort on 4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1. A count array with one slot per value from 0 to 8 records how many times each appears: one 1, two 2s, two 3s, one 4 and one 8. Reading the counts from left to right writes out 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8.

elements.text: Counting sort: count, then write back
elements.originalText: Counting sort: count, then write back

items: Find the largest value, `max`, and make a `count` array of size `max + 1`, all zeros.
Go through the values: for each `x`, add one to `count[x]`.
Walk `count` from 0 to `max`, writing each value `v` back into the array `count[v]` times.

blocks.caption: Count every value, then write the values back in order.

blocks.text: **Time O(n + k), space O(k)**, where k is the largest value. Brilliant when k is small (ages, grades, letters, digits); hopeless when values reach a billion. Negative values work by shifting everything by the minimum. To sort records by a small key **stably**, turn the counts into running totals that say where each key's block starts, then place records in order — that version is the building block of radix sort.

Radix sort handles bigger numbers by sorting **one digit at a time**, from the ones digit up. Each round is a stable bucket pass on a single digit (only 10 buckets), and stability is what makes it work: after sorting by the tens digit, numbers with equal tens digits stay in the order the ones-digit round left them.

items: Find the number of digits d of the largest value.
For each digit position, from ones upward: put every number into bucket 0–9 by that digit, keeping arrival order, then read the buckets back in order.
After the last digit the array is sorted.

blocks.caption: One round per digit: drop each number into its digit's bucket, then read the buckets back.

blocks.text: **Time O(d · (n + b)), space O(n + b)** for d digits in base b. For 32-bit integers d is fixed, so it's linear in n. Radix sort shines on huge arrays of fixed-width keys — integers, IDs, fixed-length strings.

rows.timeWhy: One pass to count the **n** values, one over the **k** possible values to write them out.
**d** stable passes, one per digit, each over n values and **b** buckets.
rows.spaceWhy: An output buffer and **b** digit counters.

items: Both are **stable** (counting sort in its running-total form) and **not in-place**.
**Bucket sort** is a cousin: spread values evenly into buckets by range, sort each small bucket, and concatenate. Maximum Gap, later in this course, uses the bucket idea.
They need integer-like keys; for anything that can only be compared, you're back to O(n log n).
**Counting sort** tallies how many of each value there are, then writes them back: **O(n + k)**.
**Radix sort** runs a stable bucket pass per digit, least significant first: **O(d · (n + b))**.
They beat O(n log n) by using values as indexes instead of comparing — which only works for small or fixed-width integer keys.
